questions.text: A sodium atom (Na) loses one electron to become a sodium ion (Na+). Which row CORRECTLY describes the difference between the atom and the ion?
options: The ion has one less proton than the atom and is now smaller
The ion has the same number of protons but one less electron, giving it a +1 charge
The ion has one more electron than the atom and is now negatively charged
The ion has one more neutron than the atom and is heavier
questions.expectedAnswer: The ion has the same number of protons but one less electron, giving it a +1 charge
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer describes the loss of an electron giving a +1 charge.

Here's why:
Ions form when atoms LOSE or GAIN electrons — protons and neutrons are not changed in normal chemistry.
Sodium has 11 protons. It loses 1 electron to become Na+, so it now has 11 protons and 10 electrons, giving an overall charge of +1.
A common mistake is to think the number of protons changes — but if protons changed it would be a different element.
Exam tip: 'Lose electrons → positive (cation). Gain electrons → negative (anion).'

questions.text: The element magnesium has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. Magnesium reacts to form the ion Mg²⁺. How many protons, neutrons, and electrons are in ONE Mg²⁺ ion?
options: 12 protons, 12 neutrons, 12 electrons
12 protons, 12 neutrons, 10 electrons
12 protons, 24 neutrons, 10 electrons
10 protons, 12 neutrons, 12 electrons
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is 12 protons, 12 neutrons, 10 electrons.

Here's why:
Atomic number = 12 → 12 protons.
Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 24 − 12 = 12.
Mg²⁺ has lost 2 electrons, so it has 12 − 2 = 10 electrons (giving it a +2 charge).
A very common mistake is to forget to subtract electrons when an atom becomes a positive ion.
Exam tip: only ELECTRONS change when ions form.

questions.text: A student mixes two clear, colourless liquids in a beaker. Which combination of observations BEST shows that a CHEMICAL change has happened, rather than just a physical change?
options: The liquid level rises in the beaker
The mixture becomes warmer AND a white solid (precipitate) forms
The mixture becomes a slightly different shade
Some of the liquid evaporates after several days
questions.expectedAnswer: The mixture becomes warmer AND a white solid (precipitate) forms
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the warmer + precipitate option.

Here's why:
Key signs of a chemical reaction include: temperature change (energy is released or absorbed), colour change, gas bubbles, precipitate formation, light or sound, and a new smell.
Two of these signs together (temperature rise AND a precipitate forming) are very strong evidence of a chemical reaction.
Level rising and evaporating are physical changes only.
Exam tip: physical changes can be reversed easily; chemical changes form new substances.

questions.text:
A student adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid. The reaction is:

magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

Which of these correctly describes the type of reaction AND a way of testing the gas produced?
options: Neutralisation; test by adding limewater (turns cloudy)
Acid + metal reaction; test by holding a lit splint at the mouth of the tube — a 'pop' confirms hydrogen
Combustion; test by relighting a glowing splint — it relights for oxygen
Decomposition; test using damp red litmus paper — turns blue for ammonia
questions.expectedAnswer: Acid + metal reaction; test by holding a lit splint at the mouth of the tube — a 'pop' confirms hydrogen
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is acid + metal, with the lit splint 'pop' test.

Here's why:
The general rule is acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. This is NOT neutralisation (which is acid + base/alkali → salt + water — no metal).
Hydrogen gas burns with a small explosive 'squeaky pop' when a lit splint is held at the mouth of the test tube.
Limewater is the test for CO2, glowing splint relighting is for oxygen, and damp red litmus turning blue tests for ammonia.
Exam tip: each gas has its own characteristic test — memorise all four.

questions.text:
A student measures the pH of four substances using universal indicator: Substance A (pH 2), Substance B (pH 6), Substance C (pH 8), Substance D (pH 13).

Which row of statements is CORRECT?
options: A is a strong acid, B is a weak acid, C is a weak alkali, D is a strong alkali
A is the most alkaline, D is the most acidic
All four are acidic because they contain hydrogen
Only D is a base because its pH is higher than 12
questions.expectedAnswer: A is a strong acid, B is a weak acid, C is a weak alkali, D is a strong alkali
questions.markingGuide:
The correct answer is the option ordering A→D from strong acid → strong alkali.

Here's why:
pH 0–6 is acidic (closer to 0 = stronger acid), pH 7 is neutral, pH 8–14 is alkaline (closer to 14 = stronger alkali).
A (pH 2) and B (pH 6) are both acids but A is much stronger than B.
C (pH 8) is a weak alkali, D (pH 13) is a strong alkali.
Exam tip: pH is a logarithmic scale — pH 2 is TEN times more acidic than pH 3, not just 'a bit more'.

questions.text: A student has a mixture of sand, salt, and iron filings. Describe a complete procedure to obtain pure dry samples of EACH of the three substances. For each step, name the technique used AND explain WHY it works (refer to the property being used to separate).
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark per step IF the technique is named AND the property used is explained. 3 steps required.

Step 1 — MAGNETISM: hold a magnet (or wrap a magnet in plastic and dip into the mixture) to remove the iron filings. Works because iron is magnetic but salt and sand are not.

Step 2 — DISSOLVING then FILTRATION: add water to the remaining mixture and stir; salt dissolves but sand does not (different solubility). Pour through filter paper in a funnel — sand stays as the residue, salt solution passes through as the filtrate.

Step 3 — EVAPORATION/CRYSTALLISATION: heat the salt solution (or leave it in a warm place) so the water evaporates, leaving pure dry salt crystals behind. Works because water has a much lower boiling point than salt.

Make sure the order is correct (magnet FIRST — once you add water you can't easily get the iron out).

Do not award the mark for naming the technique without explaining why it works.

questions.text:
Geothermal water in Rotorua is naturally acidic because hydrogen sulphide (H₂S), carbon dioxide (CO₂) and sulphur dioxide (SO₂) gases dissolve in it. Engineers find that the metal pipes carrying this water need to be replaced regularly.

Explain in detail WHY the geothermal water damages the metal pipes. Your answer must:
• identify the type of chemical reaction taking place
• name the products formed (in general terms)
• describe ONE observable sign of this reaction
• suggest ONE way engineers could reduce the damage.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark for identifying the reaction type and products: this is an ACID + METAL reaction (or 'corrosion'). The general equation is acid + metal → salt + hydrogen gas. Over time the metal of the pipe is gradually eaten away (oxidised) and dissolves into the water as a salt.

1 mark for an observable sign AND a sensible engineering solution.

Observable signs (any one): bubbles of gas (hydrogen) on the inside of the pipe; pipe walls becoming pitted, thinner, and discoloured; rust-coloured deposits in the water; eventual leaks.

Engineering solutions (any one): use corrosion-resistant materials such as plastic (PVC, polyethylene), stainless steel, or specially coated pipes; add a protective lining to the inside of the pipe; reduce the acidity of the water before it enters the pipes; replace pipes on a regular maintenance schedule.

Exam tip: Rotorua's buildings and signs show the same effect — the acidic atmosphere quickly weathers metal.

questions.text:
Compare ionic and covalent bonding using sodium chloride (NaCl) and water (H₂O) as examples. In your answer you must:
• describe what happens to electrons in EACH type of bond
• explain TWO different physical properties (e.g. melting point, electrical conductivity, hardness) that result from the bonding
• link each property back to the bonding to explain WHY it is the way it is.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark — Ionic bonding (NaCl): electrons are TRANSFERRED from a metal atom (sodium) to a non-metal atom (chlorine), forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a giant 3D lattice.

1 mark — Covalent bonding (H₂O): electrons are SHARED between non-metal atoms (oxygen and hydrogen), forming small discrete molecules with weak forces between separate molecules.

1 mark — TWO physical properties linked to bonding:

Melting point — NaCl has a very high melting point (~801 °C) because lots of energy is needed to break the strong electrostatic attractions throughout the giant lattice. Water melts at 0 °C because only the weak forces between molecules need to be overcome (the covalent bonds inside the molecule stay intact).

Electrical conductivity — solid NaCl does not conduct (ions are fixed in place), but molten or dissolved NaCl conducts electricity because the ions become free to move and carry charge. Water is a covalent compound and pure water hardly conducts at all because there are no free charged particles.

Other valid properties: hardness/brittleness of NaCl crystals, low boiling point of water, solubility behaviour.

Exam tip: ALWAYS explain physical properties by referring back to the BONDS holding the particles together — that is what excellence-level answers do.

questions.text:
Ocean acidification is a growing concern in NZ. Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid:

carbon dioxide + water → carbonic acid

Shellfish such as pāua and green-lipped mussels build their shells from calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).

Explain how ocean acidification could affect these shellfish. Your answer MUST include:
• how the ocean's pH changes when more CO₂ dissolves
• the chemical reaction between an acid and a carbonate (acid + carbonate → ?)
• why this is harmful to shellfish at different life stages
• one social or economic impact on New Zealand.
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark — pH change: more CO₂ dissolving means more carbonic acid forms, which slightly LOWERS the pH of seawater (makes it more acidic). Even a 0.1 unit drop is significant on the logarithmic pH scale.

1 mark — Chemical reaction with carbonate AND impact on shellfish: acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. So acidic seawater chemically attacks calcium carbonate shells, dissolving and weakening them. Adult shellfish struggle to build/maintain shells, while LARVAL shellfish (which have very thin shells) often die before they can grow — collapsing the next generation. (Mention of larvae or juvenile shellfish is what lifts this above achieved.)

1 mark — NZ social/economic impact: NZ's aquaculture industry (especially green-lipped mussels and pāua) is worth hundreds of millions of dollars in exports; ocean acidification threatens jobs in coastal towns like Coromandel and Marlborough; Māori customary fisheries (kaimoana) are also at risk, affecting cultural practices and food security.

Exam tip: excellence answers connect chemistry to biology AND to NZ society — show those links explicitly.

questions.text:
A student investigates the reaction between magnesium ribbon and hydrochloric acid at three different concentrations. They measure the time taken for the magnesium to dissolve completely.

Results are shown in the graph above.

(a) Calculate the rate of reaction at EACH concentration in 'cm of Mg per second' if the magnesium ribbon was 6 cm long. Show your working.
(b) Explain, using particle theory, WHY increasing the concentration of acid speeds up the reaction.
(c) The student wants to repeat the experiment to show that TEMPERATURE also affects the rate. State ONE variable they must keep CONSTANT (a 'control' variable) and explain why.
(d) Write the WORD equation AND a balanced symbol equation for this reaction.

graph.title: Time for Magnesium to Dissolve at Different Acid Concentrations

questions.markingGuide:
1 mark (a) — RATE = length / time for each:
0.5 mol/L: 6 cm / 120 s = 0.05 cm/s
1.0 mol/L: 6 cm / 60 s = 0.10 cm/s
2.0 mol/L: 6 cm / 30 s = 0.20 cm/s
Must show working and units.

1 mark (b) — Particle theory: a higher concentration of acid means MORE acid particles (H⁺ ions) per unit volume. This means more frequent collisions between acid particles and the surface of the magnesium, and more of those collisions are successful per second, so the rate of reaction increases. Must use the words 'particles', 'collisions' and 'concentration'.

1 mark (c) — Control variable: examples (any ONE with reason) — same length/mass of magnesium ribbon (so the amount of reactant is identical), same volume of acid (so the depth of liquid covering the metal is the same), same surface area of the metal (so the number of collision sites is identical), same starting temperature in the temperature experiment except for the variable being changed. Reason must explain WHY.

1 mark (d) — Equations:
Word: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
Symbol (balanced): Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
Both required for the mark. Accept clearly correct balancing only.

Exam tip: excellence-level chemistry questions often combine calculations, particle theory and 'fair test' design — be ready to do all three in one answer.
